questions.question: Describe the two main families of crane design a team could sketch, and explain what each sketch must show and how it is checked against the brief.
questions.expected_answer: The jib or tower crane has a tall mast with a horizontal arm that pivots round the mast, lifting the load straight up on a string and swinging it sideways to the bin; the luffing or boom crane has an arm hinged at its base that tips up and down so the load moves in an arc, with a second movement to reach the bin; a gantry runs a trolley along a beam between two legs. Each freehand sketch must label the base, mast or boom, pivot or hinge, string run, magnet position, cells, switch and counterweight, give the materials and rough sizes, and have a note explaining how the arm moves and how the load reaches the bin. Each specification is ticked or crossed beside each sketch, and the crosses give reasons for choosing the other design.

questions.question: Explain how a design sketch is made honest and useful: the mechanism, the drawing conventions and the use of real crane ideas.
questions.expected_answer: The sketch must show how the crane works: the string running from a winder at the base up the mast, along the arm and down to the magnet; the hinge as a dowel through two uprights or the pivot as an outer tube turning on an inner mast; and a counterweight opposite the load because a load at the end of an arm shifts the centre of gravity toward the tipping point. Conventions are thick outlines, thin detail lines, dotted hidden parts and arrowed labels, with rough sizes such as a 350 millimetre mast and a 250 millimetre arm on an A4 base to show the constraints are met. Ideas borrowed from real cranes, such as a lattice boom, a counterweight or a swivel hook, are noted with their source, which earns credit and is honest.

questions.question: Draw in words the circuit for the electromagnet with an indicator light, naming the symbols, and explain the choice between series and parallel for the bulb.
questions.expected_answer: The circuit is a single series loop of one or two cells, a push switch, the electromagnet coil and a bulb, so pressing the switch lights the bulb and energises the coil together and releasing stops both. The cell symbol is a long thin line beside a short thick line, the switch a gap with a slanted line drawn open, the bulb a circle with a cross, and the coil a row of loops or a labelled rectangle; the symbols are joined with ruled horizontal and vertical lines into a closed rectangle and every component is labelled. In series the bulb limits the current, which keeps the coil cooler but makes the magnet weaker; if too weak, the bulb can be placed in parallel across the coil so each receives the full cell voltage, and the diagram must match whatever is built.
